::: {.puzzle}
Below is a note at 220 [hertz](glossary.qmd#hertz), vibrations per second. Take away its 220 Hz part completely and play it again: you still hear the same note. If a note's pitch is not one of its frequencies, what is it?
:::

Play the note, then the note without its 220 Hz part, and watch the wave.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls">
    <button id="nBright" class="primary">▶ The note</button><button id="nMissing" class="primary">▶ Without its 220 Hz part</button>
    <button id="nPlay">Play again</button>
  </div>
  <canvas id="nWave" style="height:120px" aria-label="Waveform over three repetitions"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" id="nSpec" viewBox="0 0 320 90" style="max-width:520px" aria-label="Strength of each component"></svg>
  <div class="readout" id="nRead"></div>
  <details class="more"><summary>Mix your own</summary>
    <div class="controls" style="margin-top:0.5rem"><button id="nPure">Pure tone</button><button id="nHollow">Hollow, like a clarinet</button></div>
    <div id="nSliders" class="hsliders"></div>
  </details>
  <p class="cap">The wave over three repetitions; gray ticks mark each repetition, every 1/220 of a second. Stems (the vertical lines): how strong each component is, at 1, 2, 3, … times 220 Hz.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

::: {.gist}
**The gist.** A note is a sound that repeats, and its pitch is how many times a second it repeats. Taking away the 220 Hz part changes the wave's shape, but it still repeats every 1/220 of a second, so you hear the same pitch. The parts that are left, at 440, 660, 880, … Hz, each fit a whole number of cycles into that time.
:::

## The pitch ruler

The stems under the wave are the note's frequencies, drawn as multiples of 220 Hz: 1×, 2×, 3×, …. Those whole-number multiples are the lines of the *pitch ruler*, and every page of this series puts an instrument on it. A note's frequencies sit on the lines. Take away the 1× stem and the rest still sit on lines of the same ruler, so the pitch is still 220 Hz. The component at the repetition rate itself is called the [fundamental](glossary.qmd#fundamental). Hearing the pitch without it is called the [missing fundamental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missing_fundamental) effect, and it is why a deep voice keeps its pitch over an ordinary telephone line, which cannot carry sounds below about 300 Hz.

Open "Mix your own" and try the presets. The stems' heights change, and so does the sound's color, its [timbre](glossary.qmd#timbre), but the pitch stays put as long as the base frequency does. Keep only 2×, 4×, 6× and 8×, and the sound repeats twice as often: the base becomes 440 Hz, and the pitch jumps up an [octave](glossary.qmd#octave).

## How it works

**A note is a pattern that repeats.** Sound is air pressure rising and falling. When the pattern repeats, you hear a note, and its [pitch](glossary.qmd#pitch) is the repetition rate, measured in hertz. This holds for rates in the range where we hear pitch, from a few dozen to a few thousand times a second (for a recognizable melody, roughly 30 Hz to 4 or 5 kHz: Pressnitzer and colleagues measured the lower limit; the upper one is the traditional limit, which Oxenham and colleagues revisit). Much slower repetition is heard as a rhythm. Middle C, called C4, repeats about 262 times a second.

**Every repeating sound is a chord on the lines.** A pure tone is a single sine-shaped wave, the sound of a tuning fork. Any repeating pattern can be built from pure tones at 1, 2, 3, … times its repetition rate, and from no others; this is Fourier's theorem, and page 3 shows where it comes from. These tones are the sound's [partials](glossary.qmd#partial), and the one at the repetition rate itself is the fundamental. The repetition rate sets the pitch, whether or not the fundamental is actually there; the partials' strengths set the timbre.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>Periodic signals and their Fourier series <span class="needs">uses sums of cosines</span></summary>

Sound is a pressure signal $p(t)$. It is [periodic](glossary.qmd#periodic) with period $P$ if $p(t + P) = p(t)$ for every $t$; take $P$ to be the shortest such time. The pitch is the repetition rate $f = 1/P$, for rates in the range where we hear pitch.

Any periodic signal that is not too wild (continuous and made of smooth pieces is plenty) is the sum of its [Fourier series](glossary.qmd#fourier-series),
$$
p(t) = \sum_{n \ge 0} b_n \cos(2\pi n f t + \phi_n), \qquad f = 1/P .
$$
The $n = 0$ term is a constant, the average pressure, usually zero. The possible frequencies $nf$ are fixed by the period alone, and a given sound may use only some of them: a pure tone uses only $f$. The amplitudes $b_n$ and the phases $\phi_n$ carry everything else about the sound's shape, and the ear is mostly insensitive to the phases.

</details>
:::

::: {.qa}
<details><summary><span class="label">Reader question</span>Is a musical note one frequency?</summary>

No. A note is a sound whose pressure repeats every $P$ seconds, and its pitch is the repetition rate $f = 1/P$. By the Fourier series above, its components can only be at $f, 2f, 3f, \dots$, and usually several are present at once. The repetition rate sets the pitch, whether or not a component at $f$ itself is present, and the weights $b_n$ set the timbre: a piano C4 and a violin C4 share $f$ and differ in their $b_n$. So a note corresponds to a period, not to a single frequency.

</details>
:::

**Why whole numbers matter.** Turn it around. If something vibrates at several frequencies at once, its sound repeats only when they are all whole-number multiples of one common frequency. For two tones, the ratio of their frequencies must be a fraction, such as 3/2; the sound then repeats every 2 cycles of the lower tone. A ratio like 1.59, which is 159/100, repeats only every 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly to hear as one pitch. Try it:

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button id="r2" class="primary">▶ 2 : 1</button><button id="r15" class="primary">▶ 3 : 2</button><button id="r159" class="primary">▶ 1.59 : 1 (a drum)</button><button id="rPlay">Play the slider's ratio</button></div>
  <div class="slider"><label for="ratio">Ratio</label><input type="range" id="ratio" min="1" max="3" step="0.01" value="2"><output id="ratioOut">2.00×</output></div>
  <div class="readout" id="ratioMsg"></div>
  <canvas id="ratioWave" style="height:120px" aria-label="Sum of two tones over six cycles of the lower one"></canvas>
  <p class="cap">Gray ticks mark cycles of the lower tone. At 2 : 1 the sum repeats every cycle; at 3 : 2 every two; at 1.59 : 1, which is 159/100, it lines up only after 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly to hear as one pitch.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

Not every instrument is exact. Frequencies very near whole-number multiples still sound like one note: a piano's are slightly off, as page 7 shows, and it still plays notes. So the rule this series tests every instrument against reads: frequencies at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch make a note.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Proof</span>Two tones repeat together exactly when their frequency ratio is a fraction <span class="needs">uses cosines and divisibility</span></summary>

Let $s(t) = \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + \cos(2\pi f_2 t)$ with $0 < f_1 < f_2$.

*If the ratio is rational, $s$ is periodic.* Write $f_2/f_1 = j/k$ in lowest terms and put $P = k/f_1$. Then $f_1P = k$ and $f_2P = j$ are whole numbers, so both cosines return to their starting values after time $P$, and $s(t+P) = s(t)$.

*If $s$ is periodic, the ratio is rational.* Suppose $s(t+P) = s(t)$ for all $t$, with $P > 0$. At $t = 0$ this gives $s(P) = s(0) = 2$. A sum of two cosines equals 2 only when both cosines equal 1, so $\cos(2\pi f_1P) = \cos(2\pi f_2P) = 1$, which means $f_1P$ and $f_2P$ are whole numbers. So $f_2/f_1 = (f_2P)/(f_1P)$ is a ratio of whole numbers. Since $f_2/f_1 = j/k$, we have $k\,(f_2P) = j\,(f_1P)$, so $k$ divides $j\,(f_1P)$; as $j$ and $k$ share no factor, $k$ divides the whole number $f_1P$. So every period is a multiple of $k/f_1$, and $k/f_1$ is the shortest one.

The shortest period $k/f_1$ grows with the denominator $k$. A ratio like 1.59 = 159/100 is rational, but its pattern repeats only every 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly for the ear to hear as one pitch. How the ear decides what counts as "simple enough", and how near to whole-number multiples is near enough, are questions of perception, not mathematics; see [pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_(music)).

</details>
:::

## What we found

A note is a sound that repeats, and its pitch is how often it repeats. So a note's frequencies sit on the lines of one pitch ruler, whole-number multiples of one base frequency, and that base frequency need not be present itself. Every later page puts an instrument on this ruler: on the lines, a note; off the lines, a clang or a thud.

## The next puzzle

Why would a wire vibrate at 1, 2, 3, … times one frequency, and a drumhead not? Start with the simplest thing that vibrates at all: one mass on a spring.

```{=html}
<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, F = 220, NH = 8, amp = [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0];
  var box = document.getElementById("nSliders"), inputs = [];
  for (var n = 1; n <= NH; n++) {
    var d = document.createElement("div"); d.className = "slider";
    d.innerHTML = '<label for="h' + n + '" style="min-width:5.5rem">' + (n + " × 220 Hz") + '</label><input type="range" id="h' + n + '" min="0" max="1" step="0.01"><output id="h' + n + 'o"></output>';
    box.appendChild(d);
  }
  for (var n = 1; n <= NH; n++) (function (i) {
    var el = document.getElementById("h" + (i + 1)); inputs.push(el);
    el.addEventListener("input", function () { amp[i] = parseFloat(el.value); draw(); });
  })(n - 1);
  function gcd(a, b) { while (b) { var t = b; b = a % b; a = t; } return a; }
  function setAll(a) { amp = a.slice(); inputs.forEach(function (el, i) { el.value = amp[i]; }); draw(); }
  document.getElementById("nPure").addEventListener("click", function () { setAll([1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]); });
  document.getElementById("nBright").addEventListener("click", function () { setAll([1, 1 / 2, 1 / 3, 1 / 4, 1 / 5, 1 / 6, 1 / 7, 1 / 8]); playMix(); });
  document.getElementById("nHollow").addEventListener("click", function () { setAll([1, 0, 1 / 3, 0, 1 / 5, 0, 1 / 7, 0]); });
  document.getElementById("nMissing").addEventListener("click", function () { setAll([0, 1 / 2, 1 / 3, 1 / 4, 1 / 5, 1 / 6, 1 / 7, 1 / 8]); playMix(); });
  function fadeOut(b, s) { var dd = b.getChannelData(0), k = Math.floor(s * b.sampleRate); for (var i = 0; i < k; i++) dd[dd.length - 1 - i] *= i / k; return b; }
  function playMix() {
    var parts = amp.map(function (a, i) { return { f: F * (i + 1), amp: a, tau: 10 }; });
    C.play(fadeOut(C.render(parts, 1.6), 0.3), 0.7);
  }
  document.getElementById("nPlay").addEventListener("click", playMix);
  var wv = document.getElementById("nWave");
  function draw() {
    inputs.forEach(function (el, i) { document.getElementById("h" + (i + 1) + "o").textContent = amp[i].toFixed(2); });
    var d = C.fit(wv), W = wv.width, H = wv.height, x = wv.getContext("2d"), periods = 3, mx = 0, ys = [];
    for (var i = 0; i <= W; i++) { var t = i / W * periods, y = 0; for (var n = 0; n < NH; n++) y += amp[n] * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * (n + 1) * t); ys.push(y); mx = Math.max(mx, Math.abs(y)); }
    x.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); x.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--grid"); x.lineWidth = d;
    for (var k = 0; k <= periods; k++) { var px = k / periods * W; x.beginPath(); x.moveTo(px, H - 8 * d); x.lineTo(px, H); x.stroke(); }
    x.beginPath(); x.moveTo(0, H / 2); x.lineTo(W, H / 2); x.stroke();
    x.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); x.lineWidth = 2 * d; x.beginPath();
    ys.forEach(function (y, i) { var py = H / 2 - (mx ? y / mx : 0) * (H / 2 - 10 * d); if (i) x.lineTo(i, py); else x.moveTo(i, py); }); x.stroke();
    C.stems(document.getElementById("nSpec"), amp.map(function (a, i) { return { ratio: i + 1, amp: a }; }), { W: 320, H: 90, rmax: 8, fs: 8, sw: 3 });
    var any = amp.some(function (a) { return a > 0; }), g = 0;
    amp.forEach(function (a, i) { if (a > 0) g = gcd(g, i + 1); });
    var fr = F * g;
    document.getElementById("nRead").innerHTML = any ? "repeats every <b>1/" + fr + " s = " + (1000 / fr).toFixed(1) + " ms</b>, so the pitch is <b>" + fr + " Hz</b>" + (amp[g - 1] === 0 ? ", even with no " + fr + " Hz component" : "") : "silence";
  }
  // two-tone ratio demo
  var rs = document.getElementById("ratio"), ro = document.getElementById("ratioOut"), msg = document.getElementById("ratioMsg"), cv = document.getElementById("ratioWave");
  function period(r) { for (var q = 1; q <= 4; q++) { var p = Math.round(r * q); if (Math.abs(p / q - r) < 0.003) return q; } return 0; }
  function wave() {
    var r = parseFloat(rs.value), q = period(r), d = C.fit(cv), W = cv.width, H = cv.height, ctx = cv.getContext("2d"), T = 6;
    ro.textContent = r.toFixed(2) + "×";
    msg.innerHTML = q ? "repeats every <b>" + q + "</b> cycle" + (q > 1 ? "s" : "") + " of the lower tone: a clear pitch" : "does not line up within these six cycles: no clear pitch";
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--grid"); ctx.lineWidth = d;
    for (var k = 0; k <= T; k++) { var x = k / T * W; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x, H - 8 * d); ctx.lineTo(x, H); ctx.stroke(); }
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(0, H / 2); ctx.lineTo(W, H / 2); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); ctx.lineWidth = 2 * d; ctx.beginPath();
    for (var i = 0; i <= W; i++) { var t = i / W * T, y = Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * t) + 0.7 * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * r * t), py = H / 2 - y / 1.75 * (H / 2 - 10 * d); if (i) ctx.lineTo(i, py); else ctx.moveTo(i, py); }
    ctx.stroke();
  }
  function setR(v) { rs.value = v; wave(); }
  rs.addEventListener("input", wave);
  function playR() { var r = parseFloat(rs.value); C.play(fadeOut(C.render([{ f: 220, amp: 1, tau: 10 }, { f: 220 * r, amp: 0.7, tau: 10 }], 2), 0.3), 0.7); }
  document.getElementById("r2").addEventListener("click", function () { setR(2); playR(); });
  document.getElementById("r15").addEventListener("click", function () { setR(1.5); playR(); });
  document.getElementById("r159").addEventListener("click", function () { setR(1.59); playR(); });
  document.getElementById("rPlay").addEventListener("click", playR);
  window.addEventListener("resize", function () { draw(); wave(); });
  C.onTheme(function () { draw(); wave(); });
  setAll([1, 1 / 2, 1 / 3, 1 / 4, 1 / 5, 1 / 6, 1 / 7, 1 / 8]); wave();
})();
</script>
```
